parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Polypharmacy, deprescribing and STOPP/START
blurb: Recognise problematic polypharmacy, apply the NICE medicine-count thresholds and support a structured review that stops, starts and safely withdraws medicines.
question: Mr Shaw, 88, is living with severe frailty and has a limited life expectancy. He takes atorvastatin for primary prevention, plus ramipril and bisoprolol, and his BP is 112/60 with dizziness on standing. He says he is 'rattling with tablets'. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

teach.h: When many medicines become a problem
teach.body: Polypharmacy means taking multiple medicines. It can be appropriate, when every medicine has a clear purpose and benefit, or problematic, when the combined burden, interactions and side effects outweigh the benefits. NICE NG56 says people on many regular medicines are at higher risk of adverse events and drug interactions. Deprescribing is the planned, supported reduction or stopping of medicines that no longer help, agreed with the person. Plain English: every tablet must keep earning its place.
teach.cite: NICE NG56 recs 1.3.4–1.3.5; NICE NG5 rec 1.4.1

teach.h: Regular medicines and the NICE response
teach.caption: NG56: use an approach that takes account of multimorbidity for adults of any age on 15 or more regular medicines; consider it for 10–14, or fewer if at particular risk of adverse events.
Version 3 has 190 criteria (version 2 in 2015 had 114). NG56 rec 1.6.10: consider a screening tool such as STOPP/START in older people.

teach.h: A structured medication review covers (NICE NG5 1.4.3)
items: The person's (and family's) views and understanding of their medicines.
Their concerns, questions or problems with the medicines.
ALL prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary medicines, and what each is for.
How safe, effective and appropriate each is, and whether use matches national guidance.
Risk factors for adverse drug reactions (report via the Yellow Card scheme).
Any monitoring that is needed.

head: Adverse event (NG56 examples)
Medicines to look for
teach.caption: NG56 rec 1.6.2 (falls, GI bleeding, AKI); NG249 rec 1.3.3; NG148 nephrotoxic list; NG97 rec 1.6.2 anticholinergic burden.

steps.label: Ask
steps.sub: Is it relieving symptoms, or causing harm?

steps.label: Plan
steps.sub: Agree how, and plan withdrawal if needed

teach.caption: NG56 rec 1.6.12. For psychotropics: discuss falls risk and plan withdrawal, with specialist mental health input if needed (NG249 1.3.3).

teach.body: Medicines that aim to prevent future events (prognostic benefit), such as statins for primary prevention, may offer lower overall benefit to people with frailty or limited life expectancy. NICE asks teams to discuss whether the person wishes to continue them, using the person's own goals. After 3 years of a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis, there is no consistent evidence of further benefit from continuing or of harm from stopping, so discuss stopping. Think about medicines to START as well as stop.

teach.text: Deprescribing is not 'stop everything today'. It is a discussed, planned change with a review: abrupt withdrawal of some medicines (for example, psychotropics) can harm. And STOPP/START is not only about stopping: START finds beneficial medicines that are missing.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Shaw in the frailty clinic
teach.body: Mr Shaw, 88, lives with severe frailty and a limited life expectancy. He takes atorvastatin for primary prevention, ramipril and bisoprolol; his BP is 112/60 and he is dizzy on standing. He says he is 'rattling with tablets' and wants to stay steady on his feet at home. The nurse records a lying and standing BP, includes his over-the-counter remedies, and arranges a structured medication review where the benefits of each preventive medicine can be discussed against his goals, with a planned follow-up.

items.label: regular medicines: use a multimorbidity approach
medicines reconciliation after a move between settings

teach.caption: NG5 rec 1.3.1: reconcile within 24 hours (or sooner) when a person moves between care settings, and again on ward transfer or discharge if needed.

items: NG56: use the approach at 15+ regular medicines; consider at 10–14, or fewer if at particular risk.
STOPP finds potentially inappropriate medicines; START finds omissions; version 3 has 190 criteria.
A structured review includes OTC and complementary medicines and the person's views.
If benefit is unsure or there is harm: discuss reducing or stopping, then review.
Frailty and limited life expectancy lower the benefit of preventive medicines; discuss stopping a bisphosphonate after 3 years.

summary: You can now identify who needs a structured medicines review under NICE NG56 and NG5, and explain what STOPP and START each look for. You can also support safe, planned deprescribing that reflects the person's goals and frailty.

A.q: A practice nurse is reviewing four people with long-term conditions. For which person does NICE NG56 say an approach that takes account of multimorbidity SHOULD be used, rather than considered?
options: Mrs Ali, 70, taking 12 regular medicines
Mr Kerr, 64, taking 15 regular medicines
Mr Holt, 81, taking 9 regular medicines
Ms Penn, 77, taking 14 regular medicines
A.why: NG56 rec 1.3.4: use the approach for adults of any age prescribed 15 or more regular medicines, because they are likely to be at higher risk of adverse events and interactions.

whyNot.0: 10 to 14 medicines means the approach is considered, not automatically used.
whyNot.2: Fewer than 10 medicines means it is considered if the person is at particular risk.
whyNot.3: 14 medicines falls in the 10 to 14 'consider' band.

A.q: During a medication review, a student asks what the START part of STOPP/START is designed to find. What is the best answer?
options: Medicines that raise an older person's risk of falls and injury
Medicines that interact with each other
Medicines that a person may benefit from but is not taking
Medicines that should be stopped before an elective operation
A.why: START criteria detect potential prescribing omissions: beneficial medicines with a clear indication that are not prescribed. STOPP criteria detect potentially inappropriate medicines.

whyNot.0: Falls-risk medicines are a STOPP category, not START.
whyNot.1: Checking for interactions belongs to the wider medication review; START looks specifically for beneficial medicines that are missing.
whyNot.3: Perioperative medicine plans are not what START screens for.

A.q: Mr Diaz, 79, is admitted to hospital from home with 11 regular medicines. Within what time does NICE NG5 say medicines reconciliation should be carried out?
options: Within 72 hours
Within 48 hours
Before discharge
Within 24 hours
A.why: NG5 rec 1.3.1: carry out medicines reconciliation within 24 hours, or sooner if clinically necessary, when a person moves from one care setting to another, such as admission to hospital.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is too long; NICE gives 24 hours or sooner.
whyNot.1: 48 hours is too long; NICE gives 24 hours or sooner.
whyNot.2: Waiting until discharge leaves the inpatient prescription unreconciled.

B.q: Mrs Pike, 76, is having a structured medication review. She mentions buying ibuprofen and St John's wort from the pharmacy. Which medicines does NICE NG5 say the review should take into account?
options: Prescribed medicines on her GP record
All prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary medicines
Medicines started or changed in the last 12 months by any prescriber
Prescribed medicines that need blood monitoring
B.why: NG5 rec 1.4.3: take into account all prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary medicines the person is taking, and what they are for.

whyNot.0: Over-the-counter and complementary medicines such as ibuprofen and St John's wort must be included.
whyNot.2: Older medicines need review too; the review covers everything she takes.
whyNot.3: Monitoring is one consideration, but every medicine is reviewed.

B.q: Mr Hale, 83, has taken zopiclone every night for years. He is unsure it still helps, feels groggy in the mornings and has had a fall. Which response best follows NICE guidance?
options: Stop it tonight and remove it from his medicine chart
Continue it, as long-term use makes any change unsafe
Discuss reducing or stopping it and plan a review of the change
Switch him to a different hypnotic at a lower dose taken each night
B.why: NG56 rec 1.6.12: if benefit is unsure or there is harm, discuss reducing or stopping and plan a review. NG249 rec 1.3.3: review psychotropics, discuss falls risk and plan withdrawal as appropriate.

whyNot.0: Stopping abruptly without a plan is not the NICE approach; withdrawal is planned and reviewed.
whyNot.1: Long-term use is a reason to review, not to continue unchanged when he reports harm.
whyNot.3: Swapping to another hypnotic keeps a falls-risk medicine without addressing whether he needs one.

B.q: NICE NG56 asks teams to identify medicines with a higher risk of adverse events during a multimorbidity review. Which set of adverse events does it give as examples?
options: Falls, delirium and pressure ulcers
Hypoglycaemia, gastrointestinal bleeding and ischaemic stroke
Constipation, falls and confusion
Falls, gastrointestinal bleeding and acute kidney injury
B.why: NG56 rec 1.6.2 gives falls, gastrointestinal bleeding and acute kidney injury as examples of adverse events to consider.

whyNot.0: Delirium and pressure ulcers are not the examples NG56 lists.
whyNot.1: Hypoglycaemia and stroke are not the NG56 examples.
whyNot.2: Constipation and confusion are not the NG56 examples, although they matter in practice.

C.q: Mr Shaw, 88, is living with severe frailty and has a limited life expectancy. He takes atorvastatin for primary prevention, plus ramipril and bisoprolol. His BP is 112/60 and he is dizzy on standing. He says he is 'rattling with tablets' and wants to stay steady at home. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
options: Arrange a review of whether his preventive medicines still help
Encourage more fluids and keep all of his medicines unchanged for now
Stop all three medicines today because of his dizziness
Ask for fludrocortisone to be added to treat his dizziness
C.why: NG56 recs 1.6.13–1.6.15: preventive treatments may offer lower overall benefit with frailty or limited life expectancy; discuss whether he wishes to continue them, guided by his goals. His dizziness and low BP add urgency to a structured review.

whyNot.1: Leaving everything unchanged ignores his symptoms and the lower benefit of preventive medicines.
whyNot.2: Abrupt, undiscussed stopping is not the NICE approach; changes are discussed and reviewed.
whyNot.3: Adding a medicine to treat a likely side effect increases his medicine burden instead of reviewing the cause.

C.q: Mr Tran, 84, had medicines reconciliation on admission to the acute medical unit. He is then transferred to a care of older people ward and, a week later, is discharged home. According to NICE NG5, when may reconciliation be needed again?
options: Not again, as admission reconciliation covers the stay
On transfer between wards and again at discharge
At his first outpatient clinic after discharge
Weekly while he remains an inpatient
C.why: NG5 rec 1.3.2: medicines reconciliation may need to be carried out more than once during a hospital stay, for example on admission, on transfer between wards and at discharge.

whyNot.0: NICE recognises reconciliation may be needed on more than one occasion.
whyNot.2: NG5 ties hospital reconciliation to moves between settings and wards (admission, ward transfer, discharge); an outpatient clinic visit is not one of these points.
whyNot.3: NICE links reconciliation to transitions, not to a weekly schedule.

C.q: Mrs Grey, 80, has fallen twice in 3 months. She has taken lorazepam and sertraline for years under the community mental health team. What is the best approach in line with NICE NG249?
options: Stop the lorazepam today to cut her falls risk
Continue both unchanged, as her community mental health team prescribes them
Discuss falls risk and plan withdrawal with her mental health team
Give her hip protectors and leave her medicines unchanged
C.why: NG249 rec 1.3.3: review psychotropic medicines, discuss the increased falls risk with the person, plan withdrawal as appropriate and consider liaising with specialist mental health services.

whyNot.0: Abrupt stopping of a long-term benzodiazepine is unsafe; withdrawal is planned.
whyNot.1: Specialist prescribing is a reason to liaise, not to skip the review.
whyNot.3: Equipment does not address a medicine-related falls risk factor.

reteach.title: Every tablet must earn its place
reteach.question: How would you explain the purpose of a medication review to an older person who is worried about losing their tablets?

blocks.body: A medication review asks what each medicine is for, whether it is working, whether it is causing harm, and whether something useful is missing. The person's goals lead: staying steady on their feet may matter more to them than preventing a heart attack in 10 years. Changes are discussed, planned and reviewed, and a medicine can be restarted if needed.

items: Older people

Version 3: 190

blocks.text: 15 or more regular medicines: USE the multimorbidity approach. 10–14: CONSIDER it.

explain.body: NG56: use an approach that takes account of multimorbidity for adults of any age on 15 or more regular medicines; consider it for 10 to 14, or for fewer than 10 when the person is at particular risk of adverse events. NG5 adds that structured medication reviews suit people on multiple medicines, with long-term conditions, and older people.

test.q: Mrs Ball, 74, takes 12 regular medicines and has no other particular risks. What does NICE NG56 say about a multimorbidity approach for her?
options: It should be used for her
It should be considered for her
It is not indicated below 15
It applies to people from the age of 75
test.why: NG56 rec 1.3.5: consider the approach for adults prescribed 10 to 14 regular medicines.

whyNot.0: 'Use' is the wording for 15 or more regular medicines.
whyNot.2: Below 15 the approach is still considered for 10 to 14 medicines.
whyNot.3: NG56 applies to adults of any age; there is no age threshold.

explain.body: Published 2023 and validated by a European expert panel, version 3 has 190 criteria: 133 STOPP (potentially inappropriate medicines) and 57 START (potential prescribing omissions), up from 114 in version 2 (2015). STOPP includes categories for people at risk of falls, people taking opioids and medicines with anticholinergic properties.
explain.cite: O'Mahony et al., Eur Geriatr Med 2023

test.q: How many criteria does STOPP/START version 3 contain in total?
test.why: Version 3 (2023) has 190 criteria: 133 STOPP and 57 START.

whyNot.1: 133 is the number of STOPP criteria alone.
whyNot.2: 57 is the number of START criteria alone.

explain.body: A structured medication review considers the person's views and concerns, every prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary medicine, safety and effectiveness, risk of adverse reactions and monitoring. Medicines reconciliation happens within 24 hours of a move between care settings, and again on ward transfer or discharge if needed.

test.q: Which item does NICE NG5 list as something to take into account during a structured medication review?
options: The person's concerns and problems with their medicines
The cost of each medicine to the practice budget
The prescriber's preferred brand for each medicine
The number of tablets that fit in a weekly pill organiser
test.why: NG5 rec 1.4.3 includes the person's (and carers') views, understanding, concerns, questions or problems with their medicines.

whyNot.1: Cost is not one of the items NG5 lists for the individual review.
whyNot.2: Brand preference is not a review item; safety and effectiveness are.
whyNot.3: Compliance aids are not the basis of the review.

explain.body: For symptom medicines that are not helping or are harming: discuss reducing or stopping and plan a review (restarting if needed). For preventive medicines in frailty or limited life expectancy: discuss whether to continue. Bisphosphonates: discuss stopping after 3 years. Consider medicines to start too.

children.label: Helping? If not, reduce or stop and review
Discuss benefit with frailty or limited life expectancy

test.q: Mrs Joan Fields, 78, has taken alendronic acid for osteoporosis for 3 years and asks whether she must take it for life. What does NICE NG56 suggest?
options: Continue it for life, as stopping it causes fractures
Continue it for another 5 years, then stop
Stop it now, as its effect ends after 3 years
Discuss stopping it, as further benefit is unproven
test.why: NG56 rec 1.6.16: after at least 3 years of bisphosphonate there is no consistent evidence of further benefit from continuing, or of harm from stopping; discuss stopping, including her choice, fracture risk and life expectancy.

whyNot.0: NICE found no consistent evidence of harm from stopping after 3 years.
whyNot.1: NICE does not set a further 5-year course; it suggests discussing stopping now.
whyNot.2: NICE advises a discussion including her fracture risk and preferences, not an automatic stop.
